The verb deal has one unifying idea underneath all its uses: directing or giving something toward someone or something. That core idea stretches into several distinct meanings depending on context. Here is every important one.
1. To Distribute or Hand Out

The most literal meaning: to divide something and give a portion to each person or place.

Its clearest home is card games, where one player picks up the deck and hands cards out to everyone at the table.

  • She dealt five cards to each player.
  • Whose turn is it to deal?
  • He dealt the money out equally among the three partners.

The structure is flexible. Both of these are correct:

  • Deal something to someone → Deal the cards to the players.
  • Deal someone something → Deal the players their cards.
2. To Deliver or Inflict Something (Usually Hard-Hitting)

Here, deal means to give or deliver something that lands with force or impact — usually something negative like a blow, damage, or a setback.

  • The earthquake dealt massive damage to the city.
  • The boxer dealt his opponent a devastating punch.
  • The news dealt a severe blow to her confidence.
  • The storm dealt destruction to everything in its path.
  • Cancer dealt a cruel blow to their family.

The typical patterns are:

  • deal + [something] + a/some + [blow / damage / setback / shock / defeat]
  • deal a blow to + [someone/something]

You will almost always see this meaning paired with words like blow, damage, setback, shock, defeat, death blow. The image is of something striking or being delivered with weight.

There is also a beautiful figurative use — the idea that fate, life, or luck deals you circumstances the way a card player deals you a hand:

  • Life dealt him a very difficult hand.
  • Make the best of the hand you've been dealt. (= Accept and work with the circumstances life gave you — you had no choice in them.)
3. To Handle, Manage, or Take Action On Something — "Deal With"

This is the most common everyday meaning of deal in modern English. When you deal with something, you face it, take the necessary action, and either solve it or manage it. It implies active engagement — you are not ignoring the thing, you are doing something about it.

  • I need to deal with this problem before it gets worse.
  • She's really good at dealing with difficult customers.
  • Can you deal with the emails while I'm away?
  • The police dealt with the situation quickly.
  • I'll deal with it later. (= I will handle it later.)

Deal with also carries an emotional sense — to cope with or emotionally process something hard:

  • He's still dealing with the loss of his father.
  • I can't deal with this right now. (= This is too overwhelming for me emotionally at this moment.)
  • Just deal with it! (= Accept the situation and stop complaining about it.)

The difference between "handling" and "coping" is context. If someone says "I'll deal with the broken pipe," they mean they'll fix it. If someone says "I'm still dealing with my grief," they mean they're emotionally processing it. Both are the same verb — the situation tells you which sense applies.

Deal with also means to do business with someone or an organization:

  • I don't deal with that supplier anymore.
  • We've been dealing with that company for ten years.
  • She refused to deal with anyone who wasn't honest.
4. To Be About a Topic — "Deal With" in Formal/Written Contexts

When a book, documentary, research paper, or any piece of content deals with a topic, it means the topic is its subject — it addresses or covers that subject.

  • This documentary deals with the effects of climate change.
  • The book deals with themes of love and loss.
  • The first chapter deals with the history of the region.
  • His research deals with artificial intelligence and ethics.

This sense is mostly used in written or formal contexts, and rarely in casual speech. You wouldn't normally say "My conversation with her dealt with football" — instead you'd say "we talked about football." But in writing and formal speech, it works naturally.
5. To Trade or Do Business in Something — "Deal In"

When someone deals in something, buying and selling that thing is their trade or profession.

  • He deals in antique furniture.
  • This company deals in imported electronics.
  • She used to deal in second-hand cars.
  • They deal in rare coins and stamps.

The important thing here is the phrase: you deal in a category of goods, not just deal them. Deal in signals that this is an ongoing commercial activity — a business, not a one-off transaction.

There is also a figurative use where deal in means to work with or rely on a particular quality or type of thing:

  • He doesn't deal in lies. (= He doesn't use or tolerate lies.)
  • She deals in facts, not opinions.
  • That organization deals in fear and manipulation.
6. To Sell Drugs Illegally

In informal and street language, deal alone — without any preposition — means to sell illegal drugs. The person who does this is called a dealer or drug dealer.

  • He was arrested for dealing cocaine.
  • She was dealing on the street corner.
  • They suspected him of dealing.

The context almost always makes this clear. When someone says "he's been dealing for years," the illegal sense is understood unless there is a clear reason to think otherwise (like they're talking about a card game or an antiques business).
7. Deal Someone In / Deal Someone Out

These phrases come directly from card games — whether you are included or excluded when cards are being dealt. They have expanded into general use.

Deal someone in = include someone in a plan, activity, or arrangement:

  • If you're planning a road trip, deal me in! (= Count me in! Include me!)
  • We're starting a new business — are you dealt in?
  • Deal her in — she wants to be part of this project.

Deal someone out = exclude someone from a plan or activity:

  • I'm tired. Deal me out this round. (= Don't include me this time.)
  • He was dealt out of the negotiations at the last minute.
How the Tenses Work

Since deal is an irregular verb, the past tense and past participle are not formed by adding -ed in the usual way:

  • Present: I deal, she deals, they deal
  • Past tense: dealt (not "dealed")
  • Past participle: have dealt, had dealt, will have dealt
  • Present participle: dealing

Examples across tenses:

  • She deals cards every Friday night. (present)
  • He dealt a heavy blow to his rival. (past)
  • I have dealt with this kind of problem before. (present perfect)
  • They were dealing drugs near the school. (past continuous)
Putting It All Together

Here is the full picture of deal as a verb:

deal (cards / money / portions) → distribute, hand out to each person

deal a blow / deal damage / deal a setback → deliver or inflict something with force or impact

deal with (a problem / a person / a task) → handle it, take action, manage it, or cope with it

deal with (a topic) → a piece of writing or content is about that topic

deal with (a company or person) → do business with them

deal in (antiques / cars / goods) → trade in something as a profession

deal in (lies / facts / fear) figuratively → operate using or relying on something

deal (drugs) → sell illegally

deal someone in → include them

deal someone out → exclude them

the hand you're dealt → the circumstances life gives you that you did not choose

Once you see this word, ask yourself: is something being distributed? Delivered with impact? Handled or managed? Traded? The right meaning will almost always be obvious from context.
